claims.evidence: This is established terminology in the field based on prior work.

claims.claim: Phase I viral lytic gene expression occurs independently of the lytic transactivator VP16.
claims.source: This initial wave of viral lytic gene expression is known as Phase I, and also occurs independently of the lytic transactivator VP16.
claims.evidence: This is supported by prior literature and experimental data.

claims.claim: Late gene expression in Phase I occurs independent of viral genome replication.
claims.source: In addition, late gene expression in Phase I occurs independent of viral genome replication (Kim et al., 2012; Cliffe and Wilson, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: A sub-population of neurons progress to full reactivation (also known as Phase II), which occurs 48–72 hr post-stimulus.
claims.source: A sub-population of neurons then progress to full reactivation (also known as Phase II), which occurs 48–72 hr post-stimulus and requires both VP16 and histone demethylase activity (Cliffe et al., 2015; Liang et al., 2009; Liang et al., 2013; Messer et al., 2015; Hill et al., 2014), and includes viral DNA replication.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Phase II reactivation requires both VP16 and histone demethylase activity.
claims.source: A sub-population of neurons then progress to full reactivation (also known as Phase II), which occurs 48–72 hr post-stimulus and requires both VP16 and histone demethylase activity (Cliffe et al., 2015; Liang et al., 2009; Liang et al., 2013; Messer et al., 2015; Hill et al., 2014), and includes viral DNA replication.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Phase II reactivation includes viral DNA replication.
claims.source: A sub-population of neurons then progress to full reactivation (also known as Phase II), which occurs 48–72 hr post-stimulus and requires both VP16 and histone demethylase activity (Cliffe et al., 2015; Liang et al., 2009; Liang et al., 2013; Messer et al., 2015; Hill et al., 2014), and includes viral DNA replication.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and experimental data.

claims.claim: The bi-phasic progression has not been observed in some models of reactivation such as axotomy.
claims.source: However, this bi-phasic progression has not been observed in some models of reactivation such as axotomy, which results in more rapid viral gene expression and a dependence on histone demethylase activity for viral gene expression at the earliest time points investigated (Liang et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: Axotomy results in more rapid viral gene expression and a dependence on histone demethylase activity for viral gene expression at the earliest time points investigated.
claims.source: However, this bi-phasic progression has not been observed in some models of reactivation such as axotomy, which results in more rapid viral gene expression and a dependence on histone demethylase activity for viral gene expression at the earliest time points investigated (Liang et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: Forskolin has previously been found to induce HSV reactivation.
claims.source: Although forskolin has previously been found to induce HSV reactivation, (Smith et al., 1992; Colgin et al., 2001; De Regge et al., 2010; Danaher et al., 2003), the mechanism by which forskolin induces reactivation is not known.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: The mechanism by which forskolin induces reactivation is not known.
claims.source: Although forskolin has previously been found to induce HSV reactivation, (Smith et al., 1992; Colgin et al., 2001; De Regge et al., 2010; Danaher et al., 2003), the mechanism by which forskolin induces reactivation is not known.
claims.evidence: This represents a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claims.claim: Hyperstimulation of cortical neurons following forskolin treatment or potassium chloride mediated depolarization has previously been found to result in a global histone methyl/phospho switch.
claims.source: We turned our attention to forskolin treatment and neuronal hyperexcitability because hyperstimulation of cortical neurons following forskolin treatment or potassium chloride mediated depolarization has previously been found to result in a global histone methyl/phospho switch (Noh et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: Hyperexcitability of neurons is correlated with changes in cellular gene expression.
claims.source: Hyperexcitability of neurons is correlated with changes in cellular gene expression, increased DNA damage (Alt and Schwer, 2018; Madabhushi et al., 2015), and epigenetic changes including H3 phosphorylation (Noh et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Hyperexcitability of neurons is correlated with increased DNA damage.
claims.source: Hyperexcitability of neurons is correlated with changes in cellular gene expression, increased DNA damage (Alt and Schwer, 2018; Madabhushi et al., 2015), and epigenetic changes including H3 phosphorylation (Noh et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Hyperexcitability of neurons is correlated with epigenetic changes including H3 phosphorylation.
claims.source: Hyperexcitability of neurons is correlated with changes in cellular gene expression, increased DNA damage (Alt and Schwer, 2018; Madabhushi et al., 2015), and epigenetic changes including H3 phosphorylation (Noh et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Forskolin-induced reactivation was dependent on ion-channel activity.
claims.source: Using a variety of small-molecule inhibitors, we found that forskolin-induced reactivation was dependent on ion-channel activity.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that ion channel inhibitors block forskolin-mediated reactivation.

claims.claim: Stimuli that are well established as causing heightened neuronal activity also induced HSV to undergo reactivation.
claims.source: In support of a role for neuronal hyperexcitability causing HSV reactivation, stimuli that are well established as causing heightened neuronal activity also induced HSV to undergo reactivation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that KCl and TTX-release induce reactivation.

claims.claim: DLK and JNK activity were required for an initial wave of viral lytic gene expression following hyperstimulation.
claims.source: In addition, DLK and JNK activity were required for an initial wave of viral lytic gene expression, which occurred prior to viral DNA replication and independently of histone demethylase activity, indicating that hyperstimulation-induced reactivation also involves a biphasic viral gene expression program.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that DLK and JNK inhibitors block Phase I gene expression.

claims.claim: The initial wave of viral lytic gene expression following hyperstimulation occurred prior to viral DNA replication.
claims.source: In addition, DLK and JNK activity were required for an initial wave of viral lytic gene expression, which occurred prior to viral DNA replication and independently of histone demethylase activity, indicating that hyperstimulation-induced reactivation also involves a biphasic viral gene expression program.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing viral gene expression at 20 hr but DNA replication not until 48 hr.

claims.claim: The initial wave of viral lytic gene expression following hyperstimulation occurred independently of histone demethylase activity.
claims.source: In addition, DLK and JNK activity were required for an initial wave of viral lytic gene expression, which occurred prior to viral DNA replication and independently of histone demethylase activity, indicating that hyperstimulation-induced reactivation also involves a biphasic viral gene expression program.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that histone demethylase inhibitors do not block Phase I gene expression.

claims.claim: Hyperstimulation-induced reactivation involves a biphasic viral gene expression program.
claims.source: In addition, DLK and JNK activity were required for an initial wave of viral lytic gene expression, which occurred prior to viral DNA replication and independently of histone demethylase activity, indicating that hyperstimulation-induced reactivation also involves a biphasic viral gene expression program.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental data showing two phases of gene expression.

claims.claim: IL-1β is released under conditions of psychological stress and fever.
claims.source: IL-1β is released under conditions of psychological stress and fever (Ericsson et al., 1994; Goshen and Yirmiya, 2009; Koo and Duman, 2009; Saper and Breder, 1994); both known triggers of clinical HSV reactivation (Glaser and Kiecolt-Glaser, 1997; Cohen et al., 1999; Chida and Mao, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Psychological stress and fever are both known triggers of clinical HSV reactivation.
claims.source: IL-1β is released under conditions of psychological stress and fever (Ericsson et al., 1994; Goshen and Yirmiya, 2009; Koo and Duman, 2009; Saper and Breder, 1994); both known triggers of clinical HSV reactivation (Glaser and Kiecolt-Glaser, 1997; Cohen et al., 1999; Chida and Mao, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: IL-1β has previously been found to induce heightened neuronal activity.
claims.source: IL-1β has previously been found to induce heightened neuronal activity (Vezzani and Viviani, 2015; Schneider et al., 1998; Binshtok et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: IL-1β is involved in the extrinsic immune response to infection via activation of neutrophils and lymphocytes.
claims.source: For example, IL-1β is involved in the extrinsic immune response to infection via activation of neutrophils and lymphocytes (Sims and Smith, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: IL-1β can act on non-immune cells including fibroblasts to initiate an antiviral response.
claims.source: In addition, it can act on non-immune cells including fibroblasts to initiate an antiviral response (Orzalli et al., 2018; Aarreberg et al., 2019), as has previously been described for lytic infection with HSV-1 (Orzalli et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: IL-1β was capable of inducing reactivation of HSV from mature sympathetic neurons.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that IL-1β was capable of inducing reactivation of HSV from mature sympathetic neurons.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased GFP-positive neurons following IL-1β treatment.

claims.claim: Inhibition of voltage-gated sodium and hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels impeded reactivation mediated by both forskolin and IL-1β.
claims.source: Inhibition of voltage-gated sodium and hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels impeded reactivation mediated by both forskolin and IL-1β.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that TTX and ZD 7288 block reactivation.

claims.claim: Activity of the cell stress protein DLK was essential for IL-1β-mediated reactivation.
claims.source: Activity of the cell stress protein DLK was also essential for IL-1β-mediated reactivation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that DLK inhibition and knockdown block IL-1β-mediated reactivation.

claims.claim: IL-1β is a novel trigger for HSV reactivation that acts via neuronal hyperexcitability.
claims.source: We therefore identify IL-1β as a novel trigger from HSV reactivation that acts via neuronal hyperexcitability and highlight the central role of JNK activation by DLK in HSV reactivation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: JNK activation by DLK plays a central role in HSV reactivation.
claims.source: We therefore identify IL-1β as a novel trigger from HSV reactivation that acts via neuronal hyperexcitability and highlight the central role of JNK activation by DLK in HSV reactivation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Forskolin treatment induced robust HSV reactivation.
claims.source: We found addition of forskolin but not dd-forskolin triggered robust HSV reactivation (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Dideoxy-forskolin (dd-forskolin) did not trigger robust HSV reactivation.
claims.source: We found addition of forskolin but not dd-forskolin triggered robust HSV reactivation (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Treatment of latently-infected primary neurons with a cAMP mimetic (8-bromo-cAMP) was sufficient to trigger reactivation.
claims.source: Treatment of latently-infected primary neurons with a cAMP mimetic (8-bromo-cAMP) was sufficient to trigger reactivation (Figure 1D), suggesting that increased intracellular levels of cAMP are capable of inducing HSV reactivation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Increased intracellular levels of cAMP are capable of inducing HSV reactivation.
claims.source: Treatment of latently-infected primary neurons with a cAMP mimetic (8-bromo-cAMP) was sufficient to trigger reactivation (Figure 1D), suggesting that increased intracellular levels of cAMP are capable of inducing HSV reactivation.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental data showing that a cAMP mimetic triggers reactivation.

claims.claim: Inhibition of adenylate cyclase activity using SQ22,536 significantly diminished HSV reactivation.
claims.source: Furthermore, inhibition of adenylate cyclase activity using SQ22, 536 (Haslam et al., 1978) significantly diminished HSV reactivation (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: Activation of adenylate cyclase, which results in increased intracellular levels of cAMP, is required for robust forskolin-mediated reactivation.
claims.source: Therefore, activation of adenylate cyclase, which results in increased intracellular levels of cAMP, is required for robust forskolin-mediated reactivation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that adenylate cyclase inhibition blocks reactivation.

claims.claim: Both the JNK and DLK inhibitors prevented forskolin-mediated reactivation based on the number of GFP-positive neurons at 3 days post-stimulus.
claims.source: Both the JNK and DLK inhibitors prevented forskolin-mediated reactivation based on the number of GFP-positive neurons at 3 days post-stimulus.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claims.claim: Forskolin-mediated reactivation is dependent on the neuronal stress pathway mediated by DLK activation of JNK.
claims.source: These data therefore indicate forskolin-mediated reactivation is dependent on the neuronal stress pathway mediated by DLK activation of JNK.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that DLK and JNK inhibitors block reactivation.

claims.claim: Us11-GFP synthesis in neurons started to appear around 48 hr post-forskolin treatment, with more robust reactivation observed at 72 hr.
claims.source: In response to forskolin treatment, Us11-GFP synthesis in neurons started to appear around 48 hr post-reactivation, with more robust reactivation observed at 72 hr (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Superinfection with a replication competent wild-type virus resulted in a rapid induction of GFP-positive neurons by 24 hr post-superinfection.
claims.source: In contrast to forskolin-mediated reactivation, the number of GFP-positive neurons following superinfection with a replication competent wild-type virus resulted in a rapid induction of GFP-positive neurons by 24 hr post-superinfection (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Forskolin-triggered reactivation results in slower synthesis of Us11-GFP than superinfection.
claims.source: Therefore, forskolin-triggered reactivation results in slower synthesis of Us11-GFP than superinfection.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing the kinetics of GFP expression between forskolin treatment and superinfection.

claims.claim: Forskolin triggers reactivation from only a subpopulation of latently-infected neurons (approximately 1 in every 3.4 neurons compared to superinfection).
claims.source: In addition, these data highlight the ability of forskolin to trigger reactivation from only a subpopulation of latently-infected neurons (approximately 1 in every 3.4 neurons compared to superinfection).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing the number of GFP-positive neurons between forskolin treatment and superinfection.

claims.claim: An increase in viral genome copy number was not detected until 48 hr post-forskolin stimulus, which continued between 48 hr and 72 hr.
claims.source: An increase in viral genome copy number was also not detected until 48 hr post-stimulus, which continued between 48 hr and 72 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: A significant up-regulation of ICP27, ICP4, ICP8, UL30, UL48, and gC mRNA occurred at 20 hr post-forskolin treatment.
claims.source: For all six transcripts, a significant up-regulation of mRNA occurred at 20 hr post-treatment, including the true late gene gC, whose expression would usually only be stimulated following viral genome replication in the context of de novo lytic replication.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D-F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-E.

claims.claim: Forskolin triggers a Phase I wave of lytic gene expression.
claims.source: Therefore, this indicates that lytic gene expression is induced prior to viral DNA replication and that forskolin does trigger a Phase I wave of lytic gene expression.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing viral gene expression before DNA replication.

claims.claim: There was a significant reduction in ICP27, UL30 and gC mRNA levels at 20 hr post-stimulus in the presence of the JNK inhibitor SP600125.
claims.source: We found a significant reduction in ICP27 (2.2-fold), UL30 (3.3-fold) and gC (5.5-fold) mRNA levels at 20 hr post-stimulus in the presence of SP600125 (Figure 2G–I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G-I.

claims.claim: Treatment with the DLK inhibitor GNE-3511 resulted in a decrease in ICP27, UL30, and gC mRNAs compared to forskolin treatment alone.
claims.source: We observed comparable results following treatment with the DLK inhibitor GNE-3511, with a 2.3-, 3-, 8.8-fold decrease in ICP27, UL30, and gC mRNAs, respectively, compared to forskolin treatment alone, and no significant increase in mRNA levels compared to the unreactivated samples (Figure 2G–I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G-I.

claims.claim: Transduction with DLK targeting shRNA vectors resulted in >90-fold reduction in DLK protein levels compared to the shRNA control transduced neurons.
claims.source: Transduction with the DLK targeting shRNA vectors resulted in >90-fold reduction in DLK protein levels compared to the shRNA control transduced neurons (Figure 2J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J.

claims.claim: There was a significant reduction in HSV reactivation and ICP27, UL30, and gC mRNA levels at 20 hr post-forskolin treatment following transduction with either DLK shRNA lentivirus compared to the shRNA control transduced neurons.
claims.source: We observed a significant reduction in HSV reactivation and ICP27, UL30, and gC mRNA levels at 20 hr post-forskolin treatment following transduction with either DLK shRNA lentivirus compared to the shRNA control transduced neurons (Figure 2K–L and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K-L and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-G.

claims.claim: Addition of a PKA inhibitor (KT 5720) did not inhibit Phase I reactivation.
claims.source: However, using well a characterized inhibitor of PKA (KT 5720), we were unable to find a role for PKA in Phase I reactivation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), although full reactivation was inhibited (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Addition of a PKA inhibitor (KT 5720) inhibited full reactivation.
claims.source: However, using well a characterized inhibitor of PKA (KT 5720), we were unable to find a role for PKA in Phase I reactivation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), although full reactivation was inhibited (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Addition of a CREB inhibitor (666-15) inhibited full reactivation but did not inhibit Phase I gene expression.
claims.source: Although addition of a CREB inhibitor (666-15), inhibited full reactivation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) it did not inhibit Phase I gene expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and 2D.

claims.claim: Inhibition of EPAC1 with ESI09 did not inhibit forskolin-mediated reactivation.
claims.source: However, inhibition of EPAC1 with ESI09 did not inhibit forskolin-mediated reactivation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claims.claim: Addition of SQ22,536 did not prevent reactivation triggered by the cAMP mimetic 8-Bromo-cAMP.
claims.source: Given that we had already found that SQ22,536 inhibited forskolin-mediated reactivation (Figure 1E), to directly test the inhibition of EPAC2 by SQ22,536 in a way that bypasses adenylate cyclase we investigated the effect reactivation induced by 8-Bromo-cAMP. Addition of SQ22,536 did not prevent reactivation triggered by the cAMP mimetic (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F.

claims.claim: Forskolin induces a Phase I wave of gene expression that does not depend on activation of PKA, EPAC1 or EPAC2 but does require DLK and JNK activity.
claims.source: Taken together, these data suggest that forskolin induces a Phase I wave of gene expression that does not depend on activation of PKA, EPAC1 or EPAC2 but does require DLK and JNK activity.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data with various inhibitors.

claims.claim: Forskolin treatment was associated with an increase in the levels of γH2AX at 5 hr post-treatment, which resolved by 15 hr post-treatment.
claims.source: Forskolin treatment was associated with an increase in the levels of γH2AX at 5 hr post-treatment, which resolved by 15 hr post-treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and C), and is therefore indicative of physiological DNA damage and repair, which occurs upon neuronal hyperexcitability.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and C.

claims.claim: The increase in γH2AX following forskolin treatment is indicative of physiological DNA damage and repair, which occurs upon neuronal hyperexcitability.
claims.source: Forskolin treatment was associated with an increase in the levels of γH2AX at 5 hr post-treatment, which resolved by 15 hr post-treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and C), and is therefore indicative of physiological DNA damage and repair, which occurs upon neuronal hyperexcitability.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental data and prior knowledge about γH2AX as a marker of DNA damage.

claims.claim: The intensity of nuclear cFOS accumulation increased at 5 hr post-forskolin treatment.
claims.source: To also indirectly probe for neuronal hyperexcitability following forskolin treatment, we also quantified nuclear cFOS accumulation and found that the intensity increased at 5 hr post-forskolin treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Forskolin treatment did not result in loss of pAKT measured at 15 hr post-treatment.
claims.source: Although we did observe increased levels of γH2AX following forskolin treatment, we did not detect a concurrent loss of pAKT measured at 15 hr post-treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), whereas PI3-kinase inhibition by LY294002 did result in loss of pAKT.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: PI3-kinase inhibition by LY294002 resulted in loss of pAKT.
claims.source: Although we did observe increased levels of γH2AX following forskolin treatment, we did not detect a concurrent loss of pAKT measured at 15 hr post-treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), whereas PI3-kinase inhibition by LY294002 did result in loss of pAKT.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Both PI3-kinase inhibition and forskolin treatment resulted in activation of the JNK cell stress pathway, indicated by increased c-Jun phosphorylation.
claims.source: Both PI3-kinase inhibition and forskolin treatment did result in activation of the JNK cell stress pathway, indicated by increased c-Jun phosphorylation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: HSV reactivation and JNK activation in response to forskolin treatment does not involve dephosphorylation of AKT.
claims.source: This indicates that HSV reactivation and JNK activation in response to forskolin treatment does not involve dephosphorylation of AKT.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing no loss of pAKT following forskolin treatment.

claims.claim: Hyperexcitability triggers reactivation via an alternative mechanism that does not feed into AKT phosphorylation.
claims.source: Therefore, hyperexcitability triggers reactivation via an alternative mechanism that does not feed into AKT phosphorylation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing no loss of pAKT following forskolin treatment.

claims.claim: Forskolin triggered a transient increase in H3K9me3/S10p at 5 hr post-treatment that had returned to baseline by 10 hr.
claims.source: Forskolin triggered a transient increase in H3K9me3/S10p at 5 hr post-treatment that had returned to baseline by 10 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: Forskolin induces a histone H3K9me3/pS10 methyl/phospho switch on regions on cellular chromatin in sympathetic neurons.
claims.source: This indicates that, in keeping with cortical neurons, forskolin induces a histone H3K9me3/pS10 methyl/phospho switch on regions on cellular chromatin.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing increased H3K9me3/S10p following forskolin treatment.

claims.claim: Viral genomes co-localized with H3K9me3/pS10 following forskolin treatment.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 3A and B, viral genomes co-localized with H3K9me3/pS10 following robust H3K9me3/S10p staining at 5 hr.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claims.claim: The percentage of viral genomes that co-localized with H3K9me3/S10p was significantly increased compared to the mock reactivated samples at 5 hr and 20 hr post-forskolin treatment.
claims.source: The percentage of viral genomes that co-localized with H3K9me3/S10p was significantly increased compared to the mock reactivated samples at 5 hr and 20 hr post-forskolin treatment (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: LSD1 activity is required for forskolin-mediated reactivation.
claims.source: The addition of two independent LSD1 inhibitors (OG-L002 and S 2102) inhibited Us11-GFP synthesis at 72 hr post-reactivation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F). Hence, LSD1 activity, and presumably removal of H3K9-methylation, is required for forskolin-mediated reactivation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: LSD1 inhibition did not prevent the initial induction of ICP27 and gC mRNA expression at 20 hr post-forskolin treatment.
claims.source: However, LSD1 inhibition did not prevent the initial induction of ICP27 and gC mRNA expression at 20 hr post-forskolin treatment (Figure 3C and D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claims.claim: The initial wave of viral lytic gene expression following forskolin-mediated reactivation is independent of histone H3K9 demethylase activity.
claims.source: Therefore, this initial wave of viral lytic gene expression following forskolin-mediated reactivation is independent of histone H3K9 demethylase activity.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that LSD1 inhibitors do not block Phase I gene expression.

claims.claim: Treatment of neurons with the UTX/JMJD3 inhibitor GSK-J4 prevented the synthesis of Us11-GFP at 72-hr post-reactivation.
claims.source: Treatment of neurons with the UTX/JMJD3 inhibitor GSK-J4 (Kruidenier et al., 2012) prevented the synthesis of Us11-GFP at 72-hr post-reactivation, indicating that removal of K27 methylation is required full reactivation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: Removal of K27 methylation is required for full reactivation.
claims.source: Treatment of neurons with the UTX/JMJD3 inhibitor GSK-J4 (Kruidenier et al., 2012) prevented the synthesis of Us11-GFP at 72-hr post-reactivation, indicating that removal of K27 methylation is required full reactivation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that GSK-J4 blocks full reactivation.

claims.claim: The initial burst of gene expression (assessed by ICP27 and gC mRNA levels) was robustly induced at 20 hr post-forskolin treatment in the presence of GSK-J4.
claims.source: However, the initial burst of gene expression (assessed by ICP27 and gC mRNA levels) was robustly induced at 20 hr post-forskolin treatment in the presence of GSK-J4 (Figure 3E and F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claims.claim: The initial phase of gene expression following forskolin treatment is independent of histone demethylase activity and consistent with a role for a histone methyl/phospho switch in permitting lytic gene expression.
claims.source: Taken together, our data indicate that the initial phase of gene expression following forskolin treatment is independent of histone demethylase activity and therefore consistent with a role for a histone methyl/phospho switch in permitting lytic gene expression.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that histone demethylase inhibitors do not block Phase I gene expression.

claims.claim: The addition of TTX significantly inhibited HSV reactivation triggered by forskolin.
claims.source: The addition of TTX significantly inhibited HSV reactivation triggered by forskolin, as measured by Us11-GFP-positive neurons at 72-hr post-stimulus (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The addition of tetraethylammonium (TEA) blocked HSV reactivation measured by Us11-GFP-positive neurons at 3 days post-forskolin treatment.
claims.source: The addition of tetraethylammonium (TEA), which inhibits voltage-gated potassium channel activity, also blocked HSV reactivation measured by Us11-GFP-positive neurons at 3 days post-forskolin treatment (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Action potential firing is required for forskolin-mediated reactivation.
claims.source: Taken together, these data indicate that action potential firing is required for forskolin-mediated reactivation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that inhibitors of action potential firing block reactivation.

claims.claim: Addition of ZD 7288, Ivabradine or CsCl all significantly reduced HSV reactivation triggered by forskolin.
claims.source: Addition of ZD 7288 (Figure 4C), Ivabradine (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) or CsCl (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) all significantly reduced HSV reactivation triggered by forskolin, as measured by Us-11 GFP-positive neurons at 3 days post-stimulus.

results.result: Forskolin-induced HSV-1 reactivation requires neuronal excitation mediated by ion channel activity. Inhibition of voltage-gated sodium channels (TTX), voltage-gated potassium channels (TEA), or HCN channels (ZD 7288, Ivabradine, CsCl) significantly reduced forskolin-mediated reactivation and Phase I viral gene expression, and blocked hyperexcitability-associated histone modifications.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C50, C62, C110-C116 collectively demonstrate that forskolin-induced reactivation depends on neuronal excitation through ion channel activity. Multiple independent pharmacological inhibitors targeting different ion channels (TTX, TEA, ZD 7288, Ivabradine, CsCl) consistently blocked reactivation, Phase I gene expression, and histone modifications (Figures 4A-F). The convergence of evidence from multiple inhibitors and readouts (GFP-positive neurons, viral mRNA, histone modifications) strongly supports this conclusion.

results.result: Direct induction of neuronal hyperexcitability triggers HSV-1 reactivation in a DLK/JNK-dependent manner. KCl treatment and TTX-release, which directly induce hyperexcitability, triggered reactivation that was blocked by DLK and JNK inhibitors. Chronic hyperexcitability (≥8 hours) was required for robust reactivation.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C51, C117-C122 demonstrate that direct hyperexcitability induction triggers reactivation. KCl treatment and TTX-release (which induces synaptic scaling and hyperexcitability) both triggered reactivation (Figures 5A-B), and this was blocked by DLK/JNK inhibitors and DLK knockdown (Figures 5B-C). The requirement for prolonged treatment (≥8 hours) supports chronic hyperexcitability as the trigger. The convergence of pharmacological and genetic evidence strongly supports this result.

results.result: Forskolin-induced reactivation is dependent on DLK/JNK activation. Both pharmacological inhibition (SP600125 for JNK, GNE-3511 for DLK) and shRNA-mediated DLK knockdown blocked forskolin-mediated reactivation and Phase I viral gene expression at 20 hours post-stimulus.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C52, C72-C73, C81-C84 demonstrate DLK/JNK dependence through multiple approaches. Pharmacological inhibitors (SP600125, GNE-3511) blocked both full reactivation (Figures 2A-B) and Phase I gene expression (Figures 2G-I). shRNA-mediated DLK knockdown (>90-fold reduction, Figure 2J) also blocked reactivation and Phase I gene expression (Figures 2K-L). The convergence of pharmacological and genetic evidence with multiple readouts strongly supports this conclusion.

results.result: Forskolin-induced reactivation includes a Phase I wave of viral gene expression that is independent of histone demethylase activity. Viral lytic gene expression (including late genes) occurred at 20 hours before DNA replication (48 hours), and was not blocked by LSD1 inhibitors (OG-L002, S 2101) or UTX/JMJD3 inhibitor (GSK-J4), though these inhibitors blocked full reactivation at 72 hours.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C54, C80, C90, C103-C109 demonstrate Phase I independence from histone demethylases. Viral gene expression (ICP27, ICP4, ICP8, UL30, UL48, gC) was significantly upregulated at 20 hours (Figures 2D-F), before DNA replication at 48 hours (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B). LSD1 and UTX/JMJD3 inhibitors blocked full reactivation (Figures 3—figure supplement 1F-G) but not Phase I gene expression at 20 hours (Figures 3C-F). This temporal and pharmacological dissociation strongly supports Phase I independence from histone demethylases.

results.result: Forskolin-induced reactivation is linked to a histone methyl/phospho switch on viral genomes. Forskolin treatment induced transient H3K9me3/S10p at 5 hours that returned to baseline by 10 hours. Viral genomes co-localized with H3K9me3/S10p at significantly higher levels at 5 and 20 hours post-forskolin treatment compared to mock.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C99-C102, C140 demonstrate histone methyl/phospho switch involvement. Forskolin induced transient H3K9me3/S10p at 5 hours (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B). Click-chemistry visualization showed viral genomes significantly co-localized with H3K9me3/S10p at 5 and 20 hours (Figures 3A-B). Combined with Phase I independence from histone demethylases (C105, C109), this supports the methyl/phospho switch mechanism. However, the functional requirement for this modification was not directly tested (e.g., with kinase inhibitors), which would strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: IL-1β triggers HSV-1 reactivation in mature sympathetic neurons via neuronal excitability and DLK activation. IL-1β treatment induced reactivation that was blocked by IL-1R antibody, TTX (voltage-gated sodium channel inhibitor), DLK inhibitor (GNE-3511), and DLK knockdown.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C61, C131-C137 demonstrate IL-1β-induced reactivation through multiple lines of evidence. IL-1β triggered reactivation in mature neurons (Figure 7A), which was blocked by IL-1R antibody (Figure 7B), TTX (Figure 7C), DLK inhibitor (Figure 7C), and DLK knockdown (Figure 7D). The convergence of receptor-specific, ion channel, and DLK-targeting approaches strongly supports this conclusion. However, variability in reactivation levels was noted, likely reflecting neuronal heterogeneity.

results.result: IL-1β induces neuronal hyperexcitability in mature sympathetic neurons. IL-1β treatment induced hyperexcitability-associated markers (γH2AX and H3K9me3/S10p) and increased cytosolic Ca2+ responses to acetylcholine. These effects were blocked by TTX and IL-1R antibody.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10, C123, C125-C130, C141-C142 demonstrate IL-1β-induced hyperexcitability through multiple readouts. IL-1β induced γH2AX and H3K9me3/S10p in mature neurons (Figures 6A-C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B), which were blocked by TTX and IL-1R antibody (Figures 6B-C). IL-1β also increased Ca2+ responses to acetylcholine (Figures 6D-F), blocked by IL-1R antibody (Figure 6F). The convergence of histone modification and functional Ca2+ imaging data strongly supports this conclusion.

results.result: Forskolin-induced reactivation requires activation of adenylate cyclase and increased intracellular cAMP. Forskolin, but not cell-impermeable dd-forskolin, triggered robust reactivation. The cAMP mimetic 8-bromo-cAMP was sufficient to trigger reactivation, and adenylate cyclase inhibitor SQ22,536 significantly diminished reactivation.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C71 demonstrate cAMP requirement through multiple approaches. Forskolin triggered robust reactivation while dd-forskolin did not (Figure 1C), though dd-forskolin showed marginal activity (p=0.07 by ANOVA, p=0.03 by t-test). The cAMP mimetic 8-bromo-cAMP triggered reactivation (Figure 1D), and adenylate cyclase inhibitor SQ22,536 blocked reactivation (Figure 1E). The convergence of evidence supports cAMP requirement, though the marginal dd-forskolin activity suggests possible minor extracellular effects.

results.result: Forskolin-induced Phase I reactivation does not depend on PKA, CREB, EPAC1, or EPAC2. PKA inhibitor (KT 5720), CREB inhibitor (666-15), and EPAC1 inhibitor (ESI09) did not block Phase I gene expression at 20 hours, though PKA and CREB inhibitors blocked full reactivation at 3 days. EPAC2 inhibitor (SQ22,536) did not block 8-bromo-cAMP-induced reactivation.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C90 demonstrate Phase I independence from canonical cAMP effectors through pharmacological inhibition. PKA inhibitor blocked full reactivation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) but not Phase I (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B). CREB inhibitor showed similar pattern (Figures 2—figure supplement 2C-D). EPAC1 inhibitor did not block reactivation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E), and EPAC2 inhibitor did not block 8-bromo-cAMP-induced reactivation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F). The convergence of negative results with multiple inhibitors supports this conclusion, though genetic validation would strengthen it.

results.result: Forskolin-induced reactivation exhibits slower kinetics and affects a subpopulation of latently-infected neurons compared to superinfection. Us11-GFP synthesis appeared at 48 hours and peaked at 72 hours post-forskolin, while superinfection induced GFP by 24 hours. Forskolin triggered reactivation in approximately 1 in 3.4 neurons compared to superinfection. Viral DNA replication was not detected until 48 hours.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C79 characterize forskolin-induced reactivation kinetics through multiple readouts. Us11-GFP synthesis was delayed (48-72 hours) compared to superinfection (24 hours) (Figure 2C). Viral DNA replication occurred at 48-72 hours (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B). Viral mRNA (ICP27, ICP4, ICP8, UL30, UL48, gC) was upregulated at 20 hours (Figures 2D-F). The comparison to superinfection provides important context, though the subpopulation calculation (1 in 3.4) assumes all neurons are equally infected, which may not be accurate.

results.result: Forskolin treatment induces markers of neuronal hyperexcitability (γH2AX, cFOS) without loss of AKT phosphorylation, indicating a mechanism distinct from PI3K/AKT inhibition. Forskolin induced γH2AX at 5 hours (resolved by 15 hours) and increased cFOS at 5 hours. Both forskolin and PI3K inhibitor activated JNK (increased c-Jun phosphorylation), but only PI3K inhibitor reduced pAKT.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C98 demonstrate forskolin induces hyperexcitability markers without AKT dephosphorylation. Forskolin induced transient γH2AX (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, C) and cFOS (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) at 5 hours. Forskolin did not reduce pAKT at 15 hours, while PI3K inhibitor did (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E). Both activated JNK (increased c-Jun phosphorylation). This temporal and mechanistic dissociation from PI3K/AKT pathway is well-supported and distinguishes forskolin-induced reactivation from NGF deprivation.

results.result: IL-1β did not induce the same changes in γH2AX and H3K9me3/S10p in post-natal neurons as in mature neurons.
results.evaluation: Claim C124 states an observation but provides no data or quantification. The manuscript mentions this difference but does not show data for post-natal neurons, making it impossible to evaluate the extent or significance of this difference. This observation requires additional data to be properly evaluated.

results.result: Background and context claims about HSV-1 biology, latency, reactivation mechanisms, DLK/JNK signaling, histone modifications, and IL-1β from prior literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C15-C49, C56-C60 represent established knowledge and prior literature cited in the introduction and discussion. These claims are appropriately cited and represent accurate summaries of prior work. They provide essential context for the current study but are not novel findings from this manuscript.

results.result: HSV-1 co-opts neuronal hyperexcitability and IL-1β signaling to induce reactivation via DLK/JNK activation. IL-1β is released under stress, fever, and UV exposure (known HSV reactivation triggers), and the study identifies IL-1β as a novel physiological trigger acting via neuronal hyperexcitability with DLK/JNK signaling central to reactivation.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8, C14, C64-C65, C138-C139, C143-C144 represent the major conclusions synthesizing the experimental findings. The link between IL-1β release conditions (stress, fever, UV) and known HSV triggers is well-established (C7-C8). The experimental data strongly support IL-1β as a novel trigger acting via hyperexcitability and DLK (C11-C13, C61-C63, C131-C137). The central role of DLK/JNK is supported across multiple stimuli (forskolin, KCl, TTX-release, IL-1β). These conclusions are well-supported by the convergent experimental evidence, though in vivo validation would strengthen them.
